A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BBSplat work, with matching authors, representation, and core experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v3 includes supplementary Sections 6–7; the supplied v1 ends with references.

before.justification: v1 reports original novel-view synthesis experiments on 24 scenes, including rendering quality, speed, storage comparisons, and component ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains original rendering experiments and additionally reports DTU mesh-extraction results, hyperparameter studies, training visualizations, and per-scene results.

M1.justification: The textured primitives, compositing, density control, and compression procedure remain. Equation (7) changes the reported photometric objective from L1 + λSSIM LSSIM to (1−λSSIM)L1 + λSSIM LSSIM. v3 also reports using depth-normal regularization for BBSplat, although its retained training description does not reconcile this addition. The supplementary pseudocode elaborates existing sampling operations.

E1.justification: The same 24 scenes across Tanks&Temples, indoor Mip-NeRF-360, and DTU remain. v3 adds mesh reconstruction as an evaluated task on 15 DTU scenes, substantially extending coverage beyond image synthesis. Supplementary per-scene scores expand reporting within existing datasets.

E2.justification: v3 adds SuGaR to the new mesh-extraction comparison alongside 3DGS and 2DGS in Table 4. The comparator membership in the retained rendering comparisons, including Texture-GS in Table 3, is unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 removes FPS evaluation and introduces Chamfer-distance evaluation for mesh extraction, plus controlled threshold and texture-resolution/primitive-count sweeps. Section 4.2 additionally states that BBSplat's rendering results used depth-normal regularization, conflicting with the photometric-plus-texture objective described in v1 and retained in v3. The original splits, image resolution, and training budget remain; rerunning the retained experiments is not established.

E4.justification: Supplementary Tables 6–7 add targeted studies on the Truck scene examining visibility-threshold sensitivity and texture resolution versus primitive count at a fixed texture-parameter budget. Figure 7 adds a training-evolution visualization. The original component ablation is retained unchanged, moving from Table 4 to Table 5.

E5.justification: The FPS values with ± spreads in Tables 1–2 and the error-barred FPS panels in Figure 4 disappear. This removes variability reporting associated with speed comparisons. v1 does not clearly define those spreads, and v3 adds no explicit seed counts, repeated-run protocol, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The retained aggregate rendering scores and original ablation values are unchanged, while FPS results are removed. v3 adds sensitivity results and per-scene scores in Tables 6–8. Its new mesh comparison reports Chamfer distances of 0.91 for BBSplat, 1.96 for 3DGS, 1.33 for SuGaR, and 0.80 for 2DGS; these are newly reported task results, not improvements over v1 under matching conditions.

T1.justification: Equation (7) substantively changes the mathematical definition of the photometric objective by reweighting L1. The geometric transformations, opacity-preservation formulas, and compression mathematics otherwise remain. Removing the redundant subtraction of zero in Equation (9) is mathematically equivalent, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion withdraw the prominent claims of over 1200 FPS and up to twice-faster rendering. They instead emphasize closing the rendering-quality gap between 2D and 3D primitives while preserving accurate mesh extraction, including superiority over 3D Gaussian-based mesh methods. This substantially changes the paper's principal contribution claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of mesh accuracy relative to 2DGS and explanations of how over- and under-regularization trade rendering quality against storage. Speed/quality trade-off interpretations are removed. The original storage limitation and approximately 40-minute training time versus five minutes for 3DGS remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Supplementary Section 6 supplies gradient pseudocode, position-learning-rate decay, scale and rotation learning rates, farthest-point subsampling, sphere-radius selection, and initialization rules for small primitive budgets. v3 also adds a project-page link. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation, without establishing that every newly disclosed implementation choice changed between versions.

R1.justification: v3 adds the SuGaR reference and positions BBSplat against it for mesh reconstruction. The Texture-GS discussion replaces a rendering-speed criticism with a limitation concerning single-object scenes without backgrounds. The remaining related-work coverage is largely retained after citation renumbering.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, results discussion, and conclusion receive targeted rewrites, with speed-related passages shortened or removed. Terminology, typos, and supplementary cross-references are revised. Most technical prose and the main section order remain, while the supplement organizes additional implementation explanations and results.

P2.justification: Tables 1–3 lose FPS columns, Figure 4 loses its entire speed-comparison row, and Figure 5 loses FPS annotations while correcting Scan65 to Scan97 without replacing the scene images. v3 adds a mesh-results table, supplementary sensitivity and per-scene tables, Figures 6–8, and two algorithm displays, substantially changing the evidence presentation.

improvement.justification: The mesh evaluation and supplementary implementation, sensitivity, and per-scene evidence improve support and transparency. These gains coexist with removal of all FPS comparisons and a new training inconsistency: Section 4.2 reports depth-normal regularization, while Section 3.3 and Equation (10) retain only photometric and texture terms. The unchanged rendering scores are not reconciled with these reported objective changes, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
